editorial_title_zh: 爱丁堡电影节公布2027年举办日期（独家）
editorial_excerpt_zh: 爱丁堡国际电影节已宣布其第80届活动的举办日期，定于2027年8月12日至18日举行。在苏格兰银幕（Screen Scotland）的支持下，这一具有里程碑意义的届别将在致敬电影节悠久历史的同时，延续其在2024年由首席执行官兼电影节总监保罗·里德（Paul Ridd）及电影节制片人埃玛·博亚（Emma Boa）领导下焕新启动以来的成功。作品征集将于2027年1月开始。

article_text:
The Edinburgh International Film Festival has announced the dates for its 80th edition, set to run Aug. 12-18, 2027.

Supported by Screen Scotland, the milestone edition will honour the festival’s long history while building on the success of its revitalised iteration, launched in 2024 under the leadership of CEO and festival director Paul Ridd and festival producer Emma Boa. Submissions open in Jan. 2027.

Related Stories

Aamir Khan Tears Up About His Family, Shares Updates on '3 Idiots 2,' 'Andaz Apna Apna 2' at Singapore Film Fest

'Nobody Wants This' Creator Erin Foster on Adam Brody's Support for Palestine: 'I Disagree With Him, and That's OK'

The 2026 edition featured a programme made up of 60% world premieres, which played out in four venues across the city, and boasted a 35% increase in admissions on 2025. Among the highlights was a sold-out “Trainspotting” anniversary event at Leith Theatre with live commentary from the production team, including stars Ewan McGregor and Ewan Bremner, and a club night DJ’d by Irvine Welsh and Darren Emerson, as well as the inaugural U.K. Film Conference which included a keynote from BFI CEO Ben Roberts.

Popular on Variety

In 2027 the film festival also joins Edinburgh Festival Fringe and Edinburgh International Festival in celebrating eight decades of creativity and bringing audiences together in the Scottish capital.

“We are beyond excited to celebrate our fourth edition as the revamped and revitalised festival in August next year, as well as 80 years of EIFF. This is a major milestone in the story of our historic Festival, and we intend to do this anniversary justice with an exciting range of films, events and unforgettable moments in our beautiful city,” said Ridd.

“World premieres remain a huge priority for us as do our competitions, as we bring fresh and exciting films to audiences, industry and press. We are committed to engaging with the next generation of talent as well as established voices, providing a curated and commercial platform for work to be celebrated and found. Over the coming months we will be opening up submissions, and continuing our close dialogue with the film and screen industries, building on the successes of our 2026 edition to continue to make EIFF a place where the future of filmmaking is not simply discussed, but actively shaped. Bring it on.”

article_text:
Netflix shares skidded 4% Wednesday after mixed-to-uninspiring quarterly earnings as Wall Streeters cut price targets on the stock.

Analysts want proof of more muscular viewer engagement. They generally agree with the streamer’s co-CEOs that the key is culturally resonant, English-language series and movies that are home runs versus “the really solid doubles and triples this year,” as noted by co-CEO Ted Sarandos on an earnings call Tuesday. The biggest U.S. hits often scale globally, creating a tailwind for the platform.

The quarterly results “did little to change the narrative,” Jessica Reif Ehrlich of BofA Securities, wrote in a client note. Calling Netflix a “battleground stock” due to debate over its path, she reiterated her “buy” rating but dropped her 12-month price outlook to $90 from $105. Nevertheless, she concluded, “While overhangs are likely to persist near term, Netflix has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to adapt, execute against shifting industry dynamics and compound shareholder value over time.”

Watch on Deadline

Netflix’s slate for this fall and into next year looks far more promising than recent chatter and executive turnover would suggest, many analysts contend.

“One breakout hit could shift sentiment to the positive,” says Morgan Stanley analyst Sean Diffley in a note to clients. “We think U.S. content slate fears are overblown,” agreed TD Cowen’s John Blackledge.

Netflix’s results for the July-to-September quarter saw revenue in line, a beat on earnings, and slower advertising trickling into the current fourth quarter due to timing of ad product launches and integrations.

On Wednesday, after the release of the quarterly financials, Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters convened a town hall meeting. Sources familiar with the town hall told Deadline the execs reiterated key messages from earnings and also memos related to last week’s layoffs of 1,000 workers, the company’s most extensive job cuts since 2022.

More broadly, Alicia Reese of Wedbush Securities likes that “Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control,” she says. “Churn and pricing held up.”

She went on to note that Netflix “is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form. Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout.”

Netflix stock has drifted down toward a two-year low at around $65. That’s down by 25% year to date and over 40% in the past 52 weeks.

Why exactly is a compound problem.

First, Warner Bros. Netflix’s bid for the asset had investors questioning whether the streamer itself was questioning what would drive its next phase of growth as competition intensified. When Netflix lost Warner to Paramount, some got more scared – although mostly lingeringly in hindsight. At that moment, many investors were relieved to avoid a costly bidding war and liked the hefty breakup fee.

RELATED: John Malone Says Trump Administration Told Netflix They Had “No Chance” Of Getting Regulatory Greenlight For Merger With Warner Bros. Discovery

Netflix’s share of U.S. streaming time declined to some 16% in July 2026 from about 22% in July 2023 (per Nielsen). Its 16 Emmy wins last month also marked its weakest haul since 2016.

With the slate under a microscope, enter new Chief Content Officer Peter Rice . His arrival (after the surprise ouster of 10-year company veteran Bela Bajaria ) was Netflix signaling decisive action, multiple analysts said. They seem to accept the company’s line that Rice is the right person at the exact right moment – which will only add to the pressure on the former Fox and Disney executive.

RELATED: Netflix Shakeup: Peter Rice Is Welcomed Back To Executive Ranks While Bela Bajaria’s Exit Has Layoff-Weary Staff Bracing For More Upheaval

The new chief content officer “is a clear catalyst for change, and Peter Rice brings deep relationships with the creative community and a wealth of industry experience, having run TV networks, movie studios and streaming services. Importantly, he has demonstrated an ability to bridge creative ambitions with financial goals,” says Morgan Stanley’s Diffley.

Adds Citizens’ Condon, “We see meaningful opportunity for … Rice to leverage his deep industry relationships to attract leading creative talent, improve execution in prestige television and film, and potentially pursue a more ambitious live sports strategy.”

As for Netflix shares, there’s no way of knowing if or when they’ll ever recapture their former glory days repped most recently by a 52-week high near $117.

Condon thinks the shares are priced fairly where they are as the company searches for its next leg of growth and has a “market perform” (hold) rating on the stock.

TD Cowen’s Blackledge has a “buy” on the stock and $100 price target on a potential upswing in business.

Reese from Wedbush is at an “outperform” but cut her stock price target to $80 because the speed of a revival isn’t clear.

Diffley from Morgan Stanley has an “overweight” rating and a $77 target, citing room to improve.

Anthony D’Alessandro and Dade Hayes contributed to this report.

Featured - September 11, 2026

The Editors

Hometown , 2018

Courtesy the artist

Hailun Ma — Amsterdam

It was only after moving to New York to study fashion photography that Hailun Ma began to recognize the artistic potential of her native Xinjiang—China’s westernmost region, home to twenty-five million people and more than forty ethnic groups, many of them Muslim majority. “If you search for images of Xinjiang online, you get these very National Geographic images,” she once told Vogue . “I wanted to present a younger perspective of what is happening.” Her first major solo show outside of China gathers photographs that delight in the everyday traditions and style of Uyghur teenagers, Kazakh cowboys, and other communities sidelined in mainstream depictions of the country.

Hailun Ma at Foam, Amsterdam, September 18, 2026–January 20, 2027

Let’s Take Back Our Space: “Female” and “Male” Body

Language as a Result of Patriarchal Structures , 1977

© 2026 Marianne Wex Estate and courtesy The Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund, and The Modern Women’s Fund

Taking Back Our Space — New York

From 1972 to 1977, Marianne Wex collected thousands of images tracing the connection between gesture and gender. The result, Let’s Take Back Our Space , juxtaposes Wex’s own snapshots of body language from the streets of Hamburg with sources reaching back to antiquity—showing, say, how the pose of a manspreader on a park bench descends from the uninhibited contrapposto of Doryphoros . In this exhibition, Wex’s opus, arrayed across systematized panels à la Aby Warburg, is paired with work by contemporary artists such as Nona Faustine, K8 Hardy, and Wendy Red Star, who extend observation of everyday public space into defiant acts of reclamation.

Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 20, 2026–May 2, 2027

There’s no start or finish (detail), 2026

Courtesy the artist

Taryn Simon — New York

For over two decades, Taryn Simon has mined the hidden systems of power and influence that covertly order our lives. Father Country I Do Love You will be the largest debut of a new work ever at the Guggenheim, and the first single-artist exhibition by a photographer in the rotunda. Across forty-two works of photographs, text, video, and sculpture, Simon traces the life of a real, unnamed federal agent, examining how his individual decisions reverberated across lives and nations in ways he never knew. It’s Simon’s most personal project yet, as the work lives in the shadow her own father, who traveled the globe for the US government before transitioning into a career selling arcade games. “America is the best story on earth,” he once told her, “if you could find someone to tell it.”

Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love You at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, September 18, 2026–March 14, 2027

Couple dancing , 1956

© The Estate of Roy DeCarava

Roy DeCarava — Los Angeles

Listening, for Roy DeCarava, was far from a passive act. For his series the sound i saw , he tuned his camera to the rhythms of midcentury New York’s jazz world, immortalizing titans—Trane, Count, Duke, Lady—in his signature palette of charcoal and smoke. He also captured peripheral scenes: tender embraces, dancehall silhouettes, quiet moments of downtime. The result is a deeply personal exploration of how American life, as Ralph Ellison once wrote, “comes to focus” through jazz. Curated by Ebony L. Haynes, this exhibition brings together 130 photographs from the series, accompanied by a listening room inspired by the records DeCarava cherished most.

Roy DeCarava: the sound i saw at David Zwirner, Los Angeles, September 19–October 31, 2026

Young Pink Kate London 1998

© the artist

The 90s: Art and Fashion — London

Hoist the Union Jack: The 90s: Art and Fashion looks back at a decade when Britain’s irreverent cultural renaissance ruled the runways, airwaves, museums, and magazines. Curated by Edward Enninful, The 90s will bring together fashion by Vivienne Westwood, John Galliano, and Alexander McQueen; works by the (formerly) Young British Artists; and, of course, photographs by the likes of Corinne Day, David Sims, and Juergen Teller, who chronicled a new era of Swinging London in the pages of i-D and The Face .

The 90s: Art and Fashion at Tate Britain, London, October 8, 2026–February 14, 2027

Edge Control_edv c, 2023–

© the artist

Deana Lawson — New York

Diane Arbus has always been a north star for Deana Lawson, the artist renowned for her regal photographs of Black people she meets in various scenarios, often pictured in domestic settings and bestowed with a transcendent, otherworldly, yet sometimes strangely specific presence. Like Arbus, Lawson can astonish and unnerve. For her first solo exhibition with Gagosian since signing with the gallery in 2022, Lawson presents recent portraits that gesture to vernacular photography and Old Master painting, together with a new series called Edge Control , about the phenomenon of surveillance in beauty supply shops, where shoplifters are tracked on cameras and their likenesses posted to store windows to deter theft. Beauty—and scrutiny—is in the eye of the beholder.

Deana Lawson at Gagosian, New York, September 10–October 24, 2026

KEYHOLE 12-3 (IMPROVED CRYSTAL)

Optical Reconnaissance Satellite Near Scorpio (USA 129), 2007

Courtesy the artist and Fellowship, Jessica Silverman Gallery, San Francisco, and Pace Gallery, New York

FotoFocus — Cincinnati

FotoFocus returns with its eighth edition, The Long View , offering seventy-four exhibitions in sixty-five venues throughout Greater Cincinnati, Dayton, Columbus, and Northern Kentucky. The “long view” of the title refers, in part, to the quarter-millennium of the United States, inviting artists and viewers to contend with the nation’s past, present, and possible futures. Standouts include exhibitions by Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Nancy Rexroth, and Trevor Paglen, whose work—spanning facial recognition technologies, alternate-reality games, and AI rabbit holes—probes the dark infrastructures of surveillance and power that govern how we see the world, and how it sees us.

FotoFocus Biennial 2026: The Long View , Cincinnati, Ohio, October 1–31, 2026

Sanlé Sory Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso , c. 1990s

© the artist

Sanlé Sory — London

Sanlé Sory cut his teeth photographing car crashes for newspapers. When he acquired his own equipment, in 1960, he opened the Volta Photo studio and turned to a more celebratory subject: the vibrant youth culture of newly independent Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso). Like his better-known peers Malick Sidibé and Seydou Keïta, Sory redefined the photography of West Africa by portraying its people on their own terms. This show focuses on his rarely exhibited color portraits—images of irrepressible panache made during the restive 1980s and ’90s, when his country sought a new identity focused on anti-imperialism and self-reliance.

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years at the Photographers’ Gallery, London, October 14, 2026–February 21, 2027

Untitled (Teenagers at soda fountain) , c. 1950

© President and Fellows of Harvard College and courtesy Harvard Art Museums

Barbara Norfleet — Cambridge, MA

In the 1970s, the sociologist and curator Barbara P. Norfleet began assembling a vast archive of images from the 1930s to 1960s taken by photographers working on commission across the United States. Consisting of over twenty-thousand photographs depicting social rituals from weddings to corporate gatherings, the archive formed what Norfleet called a “unique and valuable record of American life.” This fall, the Harvard Art Museum stages the exhibition The Way We Never Were , drawn from Norfleet’s archive. Thematic sections ranging from the rise of suburbia and cultural conformity to growing struggles for equal rights centers the role of the professional photographer and commissioned image in shaping how midcentury America came to define itself.

The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection at Harvard Art Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts, through May 9, 2027.

Hostage Situation , 1979

© the artist

Flashback — Baltimore

In Paula Gillen’s Hostage Situation (1979), a young, masked child yanks a woman’s leg—clad in fishnets and yellow peep-toe heels—protruding through an unfinished ceiling. It’s one of countless gems in Flashback , an unprecedented survey of Baltimore photography spanning almost two hundred years, from daguerreotypes of Frederick Douglass, to A. Aubrey Bodine’s deadline-driven pictorialism, to the zany world of John Waters (that dangling leg belongs to Susan Lowe, a regular in Waters’s films), to younger talents such as Devin Allen and Gioncarlo Valentine who are shaping the city’s photographic landscape today.

Flashback: Two Centuries of Baltimore Photography at the Baltimore Museum of Art, October 4, 2026–February 7, 2027

23 Wall Street , 1977

© the artist and courtesy Howard Greenberg Gallery and Hunters Point Press

Baldwin Lee — New York

Raised in New York’s Chinatown, Baldwin Lee studied with Walker Evans at Yale in the early 1970s. He would return to New York in the following years to photograph the city’s empty, early-morning streets with a 4-by-5 camera. These images, which resonate with German photographer Thomas Struth’s similarly unpeopled streetscapes from the same era, were printed in 2025 for this exhibition at Howard Greenberg Gallery, which previously presented Lee’s now-celebrated large-format portraits made in the 1980s on road trips through the American South. Lee’s portrayal of New York shows how both the skyline and the sidewalk have changed, as in his image of seemingly abandoned Financial Center lofts beneath the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center—a monument to a bygone era.

Baldwin Lee: New York at Howard Greenberg Gallery, New York, September 18–October 31, 2026

Pledge of Allegiance, 1899 , 2017

Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

Arthur Jafa — New York

Named for the pioneering jazz drummer Tony Williams, Arthur Jafa’s exhibition I Am Tony presents video installations, paintings, photographs, and sculptures across two floors of the recently expanded New Museum. Renowned for his trenchant explorations of race and American culture, the artist will premiere new works alongside searing video montages including Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) and The White Album (2019), as well as early works such as the photograph Monster (1988), an unflinching self-portrait of the artist as a young man.

Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony at the New Museum, New York, September 24, 2026–January 3, 2027

Untitled , 2004, from the series

the eyes the ears

Courtesy the artist

Japanese Women Photographers — New York

A much-needed counterpoint to the male-centric canon of Japanese photography, I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reframes the history of the medium through the work of twenty-eight intergenerational artists. Presented in partnership with Aperture in conjunction with the 2024 monograph , this exhibition is curated by the book’s editors, Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko. I’m So Happy spans the medium from installations to photobooks, providing an indispensable introduction to the contributions of Japanese women to photography by showcasing intimate observations of everyday life, critical perspectives on history, and radical experiments with form.

I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now at International Center of Photography, New York, October 15, 2026–January 11, 2027.

Crosby Street and Grand Street, New York, New York ,

February 24, 1974 , from

Uncommon Places (Aperture, 1982)

© the artist and courtesy 303 Gallery, New York

Aperture Loves New York — New York

Aperture Loves New York pays tribute to photographers who have shaped—and been shaped by—the city. Showcasing artists long championed by Aperture and anchored in our publishing history, the presentation brings together important and memorable photographs with corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York City. Organized by Aperture’s executive director, Sarah Meister, the installation features photographs by more than twenty artists ranging from past to present—including Diane Arbus, Deana Lawson, Stephen Shore, Awol Erizku, and more.

Aperture Loves New York at Aperture, New York, September 18–November 1, 2026.

article_text:
Cannes 2026 is in full swing, and the Film Comment crew is on the ground, ready to cut through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more. This year’s edition is packed with highly anticipated premieres from Pedro Almodóvar, Valeska Grisebach, James Gray, Paweł Pawlikowski, and many more acclaimed filmmakers.

For our fifth Podcast from the Croisette, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish is joined by critics (and programmers) Jordan Cronk, Adam Piron, and Ruun Nuur to dive into some mid-festival highlights: James Gray’s buzzy crime drama Paper Tiger (3:15); Thai director Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s family road movie 9 Temples to Heaven (11:08); a selection of documentaries including Gabin , The Match , and The Story of Documentary Film (22:00); and the out-of-body experience that is Arthur Harari’s thriller The Unknown (34:15).

Subscribe today to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.

Introduction

Simon Stone’s film, written by Stephen Beresford (Pride), details Ian Charleson’s decision to step into the National Theatre’s production of Hamlet following Daniel Day-Lewis’ departure. Scott, who so movingly portrayed a man wracked by grief in All of Us Strangers (LFF 2023), here ascends new heights with his performance. He captures the tumult and humanity of Charleson, who is dying of AIDS (his scenes with Olivia Colman’s doctor are a veritable masterclass in screen performance) while revealing the joyful process of co-creation and the importance of fellowship in embodying a character as complex as Shakespeare’s haunted Danish prince. With a stellar cast that also includes Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Juliet Stevenson, Adeel Akhtar and Peter Mullan, Elsinore skilfully shifts gear between the ebullience of rehearsals and performance, and the profound reality of life on the precipice of the unknown. It’s a stunning achievement by Stone (The Daughter, LFF 2015; The Dig, LFF 2021) who has crafted a stirring ode to an extraordinary life, the strength of community and resistance, and the triumph of art.

Kristy Matheson

Content advice

Contains scenes of sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Screen Talk: Andrew Scott

We welcome the versatile star of our Opening Night Gala, Elsinore, to discuss his extraordinary body of work across stage and screen.

The Debut

For LFF 2026’s curtain call, writer-director Jesse Eisenberg delivers a rapturous and raucously funny love letter to community theatre, featuring a luminous lead performance by Julianne Moore.

A Long Winter

Andrew Haigh’s sensitive drama transforms a snowbound landscape into a space where beauty and longing exist in delicate equilibrium.

article_text:
The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market came to a close on Friday with market head Gaia Tridente heralding “a stronger, renewed edition of MIA, with a more ambitious and expanded program,” that saw a high-powered cohort of European and global industry guests — including Banijay Entertainment CEO Marco Bassetti, Studiocanal CEO Anna Marsh, Bad Wolf CEO Jane Tranter, and filmmakers Edward Berger (“All Quiet on the Western Front”) and Asif Kapadia (“Amy”) — arriving for a lively week in the Eternal City.

Related Stories

Ben Frow Stepping Down as Chief Content Officer of 5, Skydance's U.K. Network, After 14 Years

This year’s market expanded its footprint beyond its traditional home in the Palazzo Barberini and adjacent Cinema Barberini, incorporating several new venues along the elegant Via Veneto — of “La Dolce Vita” fame — and in the process “making the city itself an integral part of the market’s identity and experience,” according to Tridente.

She went on to say that those changes represented “probably been one of the biggest transformations of MIA, and certainly one of the most challenging from an organizational perspective.”

“We have completely reimagined the geography of the market, creating a new industry district in the heart of Rome, with Palazzo Barberini as our main hub and a network of venues along Via Veneto,” she said. “The idea was not simply to accommodate a growing market. We wanted to create a different experience for our participants, with dedicated spaces for the different activities, while keeping everything within walking distance.

“In many ways, the entire neighborhood becomes part of the market. I believe this new structure gives MIA a much stronger identity and offers us room to grow,” she continued. “And I have to say, being able to experience Rome in this way is something quite special. The city is not just a backdrop for MIA; it is part of what makes the market unique.”

This year’s event witnessed several other significant changes, including the introduction of a new gap-financing market for animation series and the launch of a dedicated strand showcasing the range of financial tools available to European producers and the growing role of equity capital in film and television production (more on that below).

The market also shifted its dates to take place alongside the Rome Film Festival, as well as Alice nella Città, an autonomous festival that runs parallel to the Rome fest.

“The decision was primarily part of a broader strategy to strengthen Rome’s position as an international hub for the audiovisual industry,” said Tridente, by “bringing these three events closer together in the calendar and creating greater opportunities for collaboration and synergies between the industry and the festivals.

“MIA remains an independent international industry market, with its own identity and objectives, but I believe that having the market and the two festivals taking place at the same time can generate additional value for the entire industry, from producers and distributors to filmmakers and international buyers,” she added.

Here are Variety ’s takeaways from a busy week in Rome:

Unprecedented turbulence, untapped potential

The 12th edition of MIA marked the first industry confab to take place since the Red Wedding-style bloodbath at Netflix, which saw the Los Gatos-based streamer ax 1,000 employees — around 6% of its workforce — including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and head of film Dan Lin, whose firing was announced on Monday just hours before MIA attendees gathered for an opening reception in Rome’s lavish Palazzo Barberini.

The firings were the latest in a series of shake-ups, retrenchments and mergers — including Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to form Skydance Corp. — that are recasting the shape of the industry, with many still puzzling over what such seismic shifts will mean for the landscape of production and distribution moving forward.

For some execs in Rome, such turbulence invites a chance to think outside the box — and seize the moment. “In my world, mergers represent opportunity. Contraction represents opportunity,” said Roeg Sutherland, who is co-head of CAA’s media finance department and its international film group. “Financiers see that as a moment where people will be opportunistic.” Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+, which in the past year alone has swooped up several companies across two continents, insisted such M&As are essential for survival amid the disruptions of corporate consolidations, shifting consumption habits, emerging technologies and other industry turbulence.

“The audience is so tough that we constantly need to be looking at ourselves in the mirror,” she said. “It’s really important to have a fresh perspective. People that are going to challenge the status quo. Because the business is moving so fast.”

For European producers, there’s also an upside when pan-European studios like Banijay, Mediawan and Vuelta go on a buying spree. “In an ideal world, a group gives you business affairs, cash flow, finance,” said Lorenzo De Maio, president of De Maio Entertainment. “Because the market is so challenging, being part of a group does give you a little bit more support. And usually, the creative stays with the producer.”

European producers digging in

In a keynote speech in Rome, Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, said that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe … is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity.” That debate is taking different forms, from the ramped-up efforts of European producers to retain IP rights to the ongoing calls for quotas that would require global streamers to invest a portion of their revenues into local productions. “The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit,” Bassetti said. “Ultimately, [the studios and the streamers] still have total control.”

Across the board, producers are feeling the squeeze. “We all know that the business has gotten quite challenging right now,” said De Maio. “Distribution advances have gone down. Gaps are harder to finance …. Buyers, both in film and TV, have become very specific with their mandates. Production costs are going up.” Meanwhile, the dizzying pace of shake-ups in C-suites and boardrooms has made it harder than ever to shepherd a project from script to screen; the commissioner who greenlights a project one day might be pink-slipped the next. “Sometimes the decision is made for you,” said Andrea Calderwood, of the U.K.’s “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions, on learning to adapt to uncertainty. “Sometimes you might think you’re choosing, but often the circumstances choose you.”

“Tenacity” is key, said Calderwood, while Daniel Campos Pavoncelli, partner and producer at Rome-based outfit Indiana Productions, said that in a fickle market, producers need to identify the “one big selling point that will make a difference” — whether it’s an A-list star, a bankable director or an irresistible IP.

Still, some aspects of a historically chummy industry remain unchanged. “What we’re trying to do is leveraging relationships more than ever,” said Pavoncelli. “And that’s relationships with talent mostly, but also co-producers, buyers, broadcasters. Those relationships, which in our business are so important, then become vital.”

Italian production spend drops for first time since 2018

Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film, TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming.

That was the main takeaway from a report issued by Italian TV producers’ association APA, which noted that this was the first decline in spend since 2018.

After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates, which remained firmly in place.

The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighborhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.”

The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “The Monster of Florence,” directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025.

Finding the audiences — wherever they may be

Audiences are arguably consuming more content than ever before — just not in the ways that they used to, with YouTube, TikTok and other platforms competing for eyeballs alongside old-fashioned TV shows. So where does that leave drama producers? “Audiences are being really choosy about how they invest their time, and we need to up our game,” said “Black Mirror” and “Sharp Objects” executive producer Jessica Rhoades. “It is harder and harder to hit the bull’s eye,” agreed Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+. When it comes to Gen Z audiences in particular, “there’s just no room for error.”

Gauging audience habits to thread that needle can be both art and science. Jamie Lynn, exec VP of co-production and distribution at Fremantle, expects to see more “razor-specific audience targeting” that will allow companies to develop projects for specific demos “at the right size and scale.” But producers and commissioners are bombarded with more viewing metrics than ever before; as Rhoades put it, “Listening to the audience too much is a fool’s errand.”

“We have a lot of data,” said Emanuele Marchesi, the director of Sky Studios Italia, the original programming and scripted television division of Sky Italia. “We have to find the courage to create new audiences.”

How to do that could just come down to good old-fashioned storytelling. “I like to think that we have the courage of our convictions,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television. “You never quite know how something’s going to be received, so all we can do is take something on that we feel passionate about. The audience is fickle. You never know what they’re going to connect with.”

“More money than ever”

This year saw the first edition of the MIA Market’s new European Investment Hub, which aims to help European industry professionals navigate the wide range of financial tools at their disposal and “foster direct contact between producers and representatives from these various entities who can provide guidance,” according to Tridente. Right on queue, Rome witnessed the launch this week of a €100 million ($112 million) fund — backed by Media Capital Technologies and Italy’s RP1 Holding — to finance audiovisual productions and film distribution in Italy and boost the country’s flagging indie sector.

From institutional investors and private-equity groups to brands and family offices, “there’s definitely more money in the marketplace than there ever has been in the 25 years I’ve been doing this,” said CAA’s Roeg Sutherland, who’s co-head of the agency’s media finance department and its international film group. For investors, the emergence of new formats and the booming creator economy offer inroads into the industry beyond the traditional realms of film and television. For producers, “I think we’re finding right now there are a range of international financing opportunities…[that] give you opportunities beyond the main U.S. and U.K. gatekeepers,” said Andrea Calderwood, of “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions.

Those opportunities can take myriad forms, from financing for an individual project or slate to an investment in a company that can catapult it to the next level. There’s no one-size-fits-all solution — either for the investors or their creative partners — and such arrangements, like any marriage, require give-and-take from both sides. Due diligence not only means having “your books ready” and being “realistic about your prospects” for a return on investment, according to Christopher Borde, managing director at the U.K.’s Media & Investment Advisors. It also means finding the right partner that’s aligned with your goals as a creative. “Know who you are and what you want to do,” said Celine Dornier, a content executive at Finland-U.K. based film investment fund IPR.VC.

European verticals ready for lift-off?

It’s still early days for vertical content in much of the world, though a recent study projected that the format will generate $150 billion in revenue in global markets outside of China this year. In Europe, the interest — and investment — is rising, with German powerhouse Constantin Entertainment among the continent’s players entering the vertical market earlier this year. “Are we at an inflection point? I think the answer is yes, in terms of people’s cultural habits and why this might work now versus just 18 months ago,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television.

Digital platforms like YouTube and TikTok are beginning to invest in original vertical content, while legacy media companies are also leaning in, said former Netflix exec Kelly Luegenbiehl, founder of vertical video and microdrama outfit Shorties Studios. “Ultimately, what is their strategy going to be in this vertical space?” she asked, acknowledging that the burgeoning market is “definitely not for the risk-averse.” “It is definitely the Wild West. I think that there is no clear path for profitability — there’s no exact roadmap yet.”

It’s the prospect of getting in on the ground floor that makes vertical content so enticing, not only for investors but for creators. “Creativity is alive and well in the vertical space,” said Luegenbiehl, noting that without a playbook, her company has been “able to try things and take risks and move pretty quickly.” “In the vertical space, I like to say we’re in the business of yes,” she said, noting that the people driving the format’s growth are laying the groundwork for the successful industry to come. “If you build it, the audience will come.”

Horror hits home in Rome

It’s been decades since the golden age of Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci and Mario Bava, but if there’s any doubt that Italian horror is enjoying a renaissance, look no further than Paolo Strippoli’s high-concept thriller “The Spiral,” which is repping Italy in the best international feature Oscar race. The talk during a lively MIA panel centered on some of the trends driving the current horror boom, from the rise of digital-native content creators to the eventizing of the theatrical experience and the “broadening beyond the elevated, arthouse horror that perhaps was only for a certain audience,” said Rachael Labes, manager of acquisitions and productions at horror streamer Shudder.

Savvy distributors are honing in on how to “create an aesthetic or a brand or a character that people want to seek out,” said Peter Kuplowsky, a producer and independent programmer for TIFF’s Midnight Madness strand. “You’re not just selling the one individual horror film. You’re selling the next film as well, and the idea that you want to create a brand around the filmmaker.”

Horror has always been a way to “discover new voices and [do] good business,” noted Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of I Wonder, which released “Backrooms” and “The Substance” in Italy. So how to find the next “Backrooms”-style breakout? “TikTok’s definitely driving a lot of the conversation,” said Jonny Bunning, of “Faces of Death” and “It Ends” U.K. distributor Signature Entertainment. Kuplowsky said there’s a “gold rush” for YouTube and other online creators — “No one wants to get blamed that they missed something” — while Labes described “a frenzy toward finding the next Kane Parsons.” Still, “you can’t acquire a trend; you can only acquire a specific film or a specific director,” the Shudder exec noted. “Seeing the success and learning the lessons and investing in talent and letting a voice come through: That’s the lesson.”

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴黎巴塞尔艺博会开幕之际，三幅保罗·塞尚（Paul Cézanne）的作品已从周四在苏富比巴黎举行的“追寻逝去的时光：斯伦贝谢珍藏”（Le Temps Retrouvé: The Schlumberger Collection）晚间拍卖会上撤下。", "links": [{"text": "“Le Temps Retrouvé: The Schlumberger Collection”", "url": "https://www.sothebys.com/en/digital-catalogues/le-temps-retrouve-the-schlumberger-collection"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这三件作品——《农场》（La Ferme）、《河畔树木》（Arbres au Bord de la Rivière）和《树木间的天空》（Ciel Entre les Arbres），其合并估价为157万美元至224万美元（140万欧元至200万欧元），创作于1862年至1864年之间。这些画作将被送回这位艺术家的家乡普罗旺斯地区艾克斯，与该艺术家的其他作品一同在格拉内博物馆（Musée Granet）展出。苏富比表示，其一直在与斯伦贝谢家族及普罗旺斯地区艾克斯市进行商讨，在法国文化部的支持下，该市目前正计划为博物馆收购这些艺术品。", "links": [{"text": "Aix-en-Provenance", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/paul-cezanne-switzerland-museum-langmatt-christies-20th-century-evening-sale-2023-1234680429/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "苏富比法国现代及当代艺术联席主管托马斯·邦帕尔（Thomas Bompard）在一份声明中表示，这三幅杰出画作“几乎没有比这更合适的荣归故里了”，它们创作于塞尚的家族庄园兼早期工作室布旺山庄（Jas de Bouffan），这里对其艺术演变至关重要。邦帕尔补充说，这三幅画作“与普罗旺斯地区艾克斯有着非同寻常的联系。我们很高兴能协助撮合斯伦贝谢家族与普罗旺斯地区艾克斯市，并且——得益于他们的承诺以及法国文化部的支持——已经找到了完美的途径，使这些作品能够重返其故事开始的地方。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些画作曾是布旺山庄的重要组成部分，当时它们构成了底层墙壁上的一幅大型壁画，向塞尚所钦佩的古代大师致敬。然而，在1899年庄园被分散后，该壁画被剥离并转移到了画布上，随后被拆分为8个碎片。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Three works by Paul Cézanne have been removed from the “Le Temps Retrouvé: The Schlumberger Collection” evening sale at Sotheby’s Paris on Thursday coinciding with Art Basel Paris.

The three works: La Ferme , Arbres au Bord de la Rivière and Ciel Entre les Arbres , carried a combined estimate of $1.57 million to $2.24 million (€1.4 million to €2 million) and were painted between 1862 and 1864. The paintings are being returned to the artist’s hometown in Aix-en-Provenance to be displayed at the Musée Granet along with the artist’s other work. Sotheby’s said it has been holding discussions with the Schlumberger family and the town of Aix-en-Provence which, with the support of the French Ministry of Culture, now intends to acquire the artworks for the museum.

Thomas Bompard, co-head of modern and contemporary art at Sotheby’s France, said in a statement that there “could scarcely be a more fitting homecoming for these three remarkable paintings” that were created at the Jas de Bouffan, the family estate and early studio of Cézanne, which was such a critical part of his artistic evolution. Bompard added that the three paintings have “an extraordinary connection to Aix-en-Provence. We are delighted to have helped bring together the Schlumberger family and the town of Aix-en-Provence, and that—thanks to their commitment and the support of the French Ministry of Culture—a perfect path has been found to enable the works to return to the place where their story began.”

The paintings were once an important part of Jas de Bouffan, as they made up a large mural painted on the ground floor walls as a nod to the great masters of the past that Cézanne admired. However, the mural was detached and transferred to canvas in 1899 following the dispersal of the estate and then divided into eight fragments.

article_text:
Released in 2008, Ballast won a Best Director award at Sundance for Lance Hammer, who also wrote and edited the drama set in a troubled family. Hammer waited almost twenty years for his follow-up film, Queen at Sea .

Starring Juliette Binoche, Tom Courtenay, and Anna Calder-Marshall, Queen at Sea examines in painful detail the aftermath of a sexual encounter between an elderly couple. Issues of agency and consent become weapons that threaten to send Leslie (Calder-Marshall) to an assisted living facility. Her daughter Amanda (Binoche) agonizes over decisions that could wreck her stepfather Martin’s (Courtenay) life.

Amanda marks another challenging role for Binoche, in a career filled with outstanding performances. Both Courtenay and Calder-Marshall won supporting actor awards at the 76th Berlinale. Hammer and his film won the Silver Bear Jury Prize.

Hammer spoke with the Film Stage at Berlinale earlier this year, which we’re sharing ahead of the film’s theatrical release this Friday.

The Film Stage: This is your first film in nearly two decades. How many years did it take?

Lance Hammer : I started writing a script in 2015. It took about a year to write. I wanted to see if I could write a script that I cared about. When I finished I said, “Well, I might as well try to show some people to see what they think. Maybe I’ll try to make it.”

I immediately got a response from a pretty big production company that green-lit it, contingent on casting an A-list actor for Juliette’s role. They had a list of people that they would accept. I didn’t want to cast any of the people on the list. I panicked about it. This was before Juliette was on board.

And the script wasn’t ready. I needed to do more work on it. I usually take a long time. While I kept working it just fell apart with them.

I took the script, scraped it off the ground, and put it back together again with another great production company, one more aligned with my creative thinking. They ended up folding. So I lost the project again. That’s when I said, “I’m just going to go to Juliette Binoche because she’s the right person.” I realized the part doesn’t have to be American, you know? I gave it to the person I really wanted to do the role, someone I really loved, and she said yes right away.

That’s when the project became a totally different animal. Juliette became a producer, a very tenacious and committed one. She helped attract attention for the third go-round. She was involved through several years of false starts, resurrecting it, picking up all the pieces, putting them back together.

Then I went to Tom Courtenay because, okay, I don’t care where it’s shot. I love Tom, I want him to do the role, so let’s shoot it in London. I don’t care what Tom’s box-office value is, I’m not even thinking that way anymore.

I know this will be a small film. I’ll reduce the budget to make it with these two actors. I got in touch with Tristan Goligher with The Bureau, a production company. Suddenly it became a real thing. Tom liked the script, but he was also interested because of Juliette. And he had done 45 Years with Tristan. So that’s how we did it, but it took ten years or so.

Lance Hammer. Courtesy of Berlinale .

You start with a pretty incendiary scene of your two stars having sex.

In basic dramaturgy, that’s the inciting incident. Your story is everything that happens after that. I liked the economy and logic of starting with that. No wasting time showing context or developing the characters’ backgrounds—that’s pointless. What I would rather do is have you enter a situation with confusion and disorientation as happens in life when you encounter a new person and you see something on the street happen. You don’t know anything about their lives, but you have to learn that through discovery.

There’s another element. Seeing the sexual act between elderly people somehow feels taboo. It shouldn’t be. Why is it taboo? When you see young people having sex, it’s glorified, it’s celebrated, we vicariously live through it, and it speaks of new life and creation. Everything is hopeful and possible. Everything is in the future.

End-of-life sex, it’s like a cognitive dissonance. You’re seeing people doing things we reserve for youth, but now in old bodies. I wanted to show the act as a very banal, simple, boring type of sex. I didn’t want to titillate or provoke. I just wanted the simplest, most boring presentation.

I understood that this would be disturbing. I’m also a victim of ageist prejudice, you know? Because I’m afraid of dying. When we see older people having sex, it gives us a too-close-to-the-bone awareness of our own mortality.

Did you have a personal interest in dementia?

When I first started to outline a script, it’s like a radar was attracting all these stories about dementia. Lots of articles in the news. My father is Tom Courtenay’s age, and he has friends who were experiencing similar sexual situations. I read about the moral dilemmas facing the elderly. This all became a kind of a composite that fed the premise of the story of agency and consent.

I’m uncertain where I stand morally on this, and I bet you I’m not the only person who feels this way. I feel a great way to make a film is to start from a place of uncertainty and not try to insist on a moral position.

For example, I have a simple moral position. Tom, or Martin as he is played, should not be having sex with Leslie. If there is any uncertainty at all about her consent, if sex may be causing her harm, if she can’t communicate adequately, he needs to stop.

I also understand how a man who’s been in a marriage for 18 years, one with an ongoing, meaningful sexual relationship, one where she’s given consent in the past and apparently is continuing to do so—I can understand that he may no longer understand there is a line he can’t cross. He doesn’t know where the line is if she is no longer cognitively capable of giving consent. People don’t want to talk about it.

Can you talk about your visual approach?

My aesthetic nature is very reductionist. I was an art director on films for a while, and an architect before that. Once you study architecture, it’s forever in you. It’s a curse. So my approach is very minimal. I start with a maximalist field of possibilities, explore those ideas, then methodically reduce, reduce, reduce to its essence. The things you’ve cut away are still contained in the thing you keep. They have a ghostly or erratic presence in them. The ghost of what’s been removed is still present in the thing you keep.

I wouldn’t call myself a brutalist. That’s from a very different time. But the ethos behind brutalism, I am that.

Can you talk about working with cinematographer Adolpho Veloso ?

Our overall visual strategy was to use all static shots locked off in the house. With the teenagers, necessarily, all the shots had to be handheld because those are totally improvised scenes. We couldn’t set up a shot and have them conform to the camera. It had to be the other way around.

With Juliette’s story, we used a mixture of the two. So Juliette or the Amanda and Sara (Florence Hunt) characters interact as mother and child together in scenes. Some of them are locked off, some of them are handheld.

When the grandmother is being examined in the medical office, when does the camera move? When does Veloso rack focus to other characters? Is that a consensus between the two of you?

We wanted to show urgency, restlessness, and anxiety. Not with a shaky camera, but hold it as still as humanly possible. But the camera also has to be able to move freely. In those scenes, Adolpho is totally on his own. My role is really to talk to him about what he’s going to be doing. But my main job is with the actors and the set, which was a real examination room.

The timings and the performances, Adolpho is documenting them. It’s entirely his amazing, compassionate eye, his instinct to follow, that I needed there.

What I learned with Adolpho very early on was that we had identical ideas about how to shoot this film. We did a month of workshopping and rehearsals in a lot of the locations. Adolpho was part of that workshopping. I’d be focusing on the actors, but also thinking about camera and composition. I’d see Adolfo thinking, and I’d say, “Hey, I think the coverage for this should be…” And he’d cut me off and have exactly the same thought.

We rehearsed a lot. I told him when I need to be in focus here, when I need to rack to there. I would discuss with him when I think you need to be on this side, when it has to be a frontal approach, how to get from here to there at a certain moment.

It was uncanny how often we had exactly the same idea, which was great because then I could just let go. Adolpho took this huge load off my shoulders, and he did it extraordinarily well, I think. But it could only work because we were totally in step with each other.

Did the story change or evolve during editing?

Strangely, this one stayed pretty close to the script. Because we workshopped it so much, that’s when the changes occurred. When I was writing, the script evolved as I received information from advisors and consultants. Once the script was done and the actors came in, I got new professional consultants for advice specific to UK legal and health systems. The script changed radically then. When I started working with the actors, the scenes changed again.

By the time we started shooting, we’d figured it all out. The edit on this one took a long time, but it wasn’t because I was trying to change the story. That had already been done in the workshopping. You could call it a kind of pre-editing with the actors. A collaborative edit.

I did delete a lot. I cut a lot of stuff, which is normal.

Queen at Sea opens in theaters on Friday, October 30.

我在2015年开始写脚本,花了大约一年时间写作,我想看看我是否能写出我关心的脚本,当我完成时,我说:“好吧,我也可能试着让一些人看到他们想什么,也许我会试着做。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我立刻得到一个相当大的生产公司的回应,绿色点亮了它,紧急地提起一个A名单的演员为朱丽叶的角色,他们有一个名单的人,他们会接受,我不想把任何人放在名单上,我恐慌了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而且剧本还没有准备好,我需要更多的工作,我通常需要很长时间,而我一直在工作,它只是与他们分开。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我拿起剧本,把它从地面上拉出来,把它重新与另一个伟大的生产公司,另一个与我的创造性思维相匹配,他们结束了,所以我再次失去了项目,那是我说:“我只是去朱丽叶·比诺切,因为她是正确的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是当项目变成一个完全不同的动物时,朱丽叶变成了一个制作人,一个非常紧张和致力于一个,她帮助吸引第三轮的注意力,她参与了几年的假开始,复活它,收集所有零件,把它们聚集在一起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然后我去了汤姆·库特内,因为,好吧,我不在乎它在哪里被拍摄,我爱汤姆,我希望他能扮演角色,所以让我们在伦敦拍摄它,我不在乎汤姆的盒子办公室价值是什么,我甚至不再这样想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我知道这将是一部小电影,我会减少预算,让这两位演员一起做,我接触到特里斯坦·戈利格与制作公司《办公室》,突然变成了一件真实的事情,汤姆喜欢剧本,但他也因为朱丽叶感兴趣,他和特里斯坦做了45年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Lance-Hammer-800x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "兰斯·哈默《柏林的勇气》", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你开始了一个相当火焰的场景,你的两个星星有性爱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在基本戏剧中,这就是激发的事件,你的故事就是之后发生的一切,我喜欢经济和逻辑开始,没有浪费时间展示背景或发展角色背景,这毫无意义,我宁愿做的是你进入一个混乱和偏离的情况,就像在生活中发生的那样,当你遇到一个新人,你看到街上发生的事情,你不知道他们的生活,但你必须通过发现学习。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "看到老年人之间的性行为,就好像是禁忌,不应该是禁忌,为什么是禁忌?当你看到年轻人有性行为时,它是荣耀的,它是庆祝的,我们很生气地生活在它中,它谈论新的生活和创造,一切都是希望的,一切都是可能的,一切都是未来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "终身性别,就像一个认知分离,你看到人们做我们为青春预备的东西,但现在在老身体里,我想表现出这个行为是非常平凡的,简单的,无聊的性别,我不想嘲笑或挑衅,我只是想要最简单的,最无聊的演示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我明白这会令人不安,我也是老年人偏见的受害者,你知道吗?因为我害怕死亡,当我们看到老年人有性时,它给了我们对自己的死亡的过近意识。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你对痴呆症有个人兴趣吗?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我第一次开始描述一个脚本时,它就像一个雷达吸引了关于痴呆症的所有这些故事一样。新闻中的许多文章.我父亲是汤姆·库特奈的年龄,他有朋友经历了类似的性状况.我读到面对老年人的道德差异。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不确定我道德上站在哪里,我赌你我不是唯一这样感觉的人,我觉得拍电影的好办法就是从不确定的地方开始,不要试图坚持道德立场。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "例如,我有一个简单的道德立场. 汤姆,或马丁,因为他被演奏,不应该有性与莱斯利. 如果有任何不确定性关于她的同意,如果性可能会导致她的伤害,如果她不能适当沟通,他必须停止。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我也明白一个男人已经结婚了18年,一个有一个持续的,有意义的性关系,一个她在过去得到同意,显然继续这样做的人,我可以理解他可能不再明白有一个线,他不能穿过,他不知道线在哪里,如果她已经不再认知地能够同意,人们不想谈论它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你能谈谈你的视觉方法吗?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的美学性质是非常低调的,我是一部电影的艺术导演一段时间,在那之前,建筑师,一旦你学习建筑,它是永远在你里面,这是一个<unk>咒,所以我的方法是非常微小的,我开始一个最大化的可能性领域,探索这些想法,然后方法性减少,减少,减少到它的本质。除去的仍然存在于你所保留的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不会称自己为残酷主义者,这是从一个非常不同的时代来的,但残酷主义背后的道德,我就是这样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你能和电影作家Adolpho Veloso合作吗?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们的整体视觉策略是使用所有静态射击在房子里锁定。 与青少年,必然,所有的射击必须处理,因为这些都是完全改进的场景。 我们不能设置一个射击,并将它们符合相机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与朱丽叶的故事,我们使用了一个混合两者,所以朱丽叶或阿曼达和莎拉(佛罗伦萨猎)的角色互动作为母亲和孩子一起在场景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "當奶奶在醫院檢查時,相機何時會移動?當Veloso 拉克焦點於其他角色?這兩人之間的共识嗎?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们想展示紧急性、不安和焦虑,不是一个可耻的摄像头,但保持它尽可能的人性。但摄像头也必须能够自由移动。在这些场景中,阿道夫完全是自己的。我的角色是真正告诉他他会做什么。但我的主要工作是与演员和组,这是一个真正的审查室。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "时间表和表演,阿道尔福正在记录它们,这是他的惊人的,同情的眼睛,他的本能跟随,我需要在那里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我和Adolpho很早就知道,我们有相同的想法如何拍摄这部电影,我们在许多地方做了一个月的工作购物和重新听证会,Adolpho是工作购物的一部分,我会专注于演员,但也思考摄像头和组合,我会看到Adolfo思考,我会说,“哦,我认为这应该是覆盖的......”他会把我切断出来,有相同的想法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我告诉他,我需要什么时候在这里集中注意力,我需要到达那里,我会和他讨论什么时候我认为你需要在这个方面,什么时候它必须是前沿的方法,如何在某个时候从这里到那里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是不可思议的,我们有多少次正是相同的想法,这是很棒的,因为那时我只能离开。Adolpho把这个巨大的负担从我的肩膀上拿出来,他做得非常好,我认为。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "编辑期间,故事发生了变化还是进展?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奇怪的是,这位留在剧本附近,因为我们工作了这么多,那就是当变化发生时,当我写作时,剧本随着我从顾问和顾问那里获得信息而发展,一旦剧本完成,演员进来,我得到了新的专业顾问,专门为英国法律和卫生系统提供建议。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我们开始拍摄时,我们会想象这一切。编辑这个人花了很长时间,但这不是因为我试图改变故事。这已经在工作场所完成了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我把很多东西剪掉了,这是正常的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "海边女王将于10月30日星期五在剧院开幕。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Films and events

Journey

Tutu

Sam Pollard’s impressively researched and rich archival documentary is an incisive portrait of one of the most beloved public figures of the 20th century.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Sam Pollard

UK-South Africa 2026. 101min

Courtesy of Hidden Light

Languages English, Afrikaans With some English subtitles

Introduction

For a man who possessed an impish, joyful persona, Archbishop Desmond Tutu brought nerves of steel and a fierce intelligence to his fight against Apartheid in South Africa and beating a path to national reconciliation. Pollard’s engaging film gives primacy to Tutu’s political life, but smartly orientates this within a fulsome portrait of a man whose unshakeable belief in humanity continues to inspire long after his passing.

Kristy Matheson

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, racism, and racist violence.

How to book

Art Review

Lisa Sanditz’s Seismic Sublime

Her environmental paintings ask: What can we do to change our destiny? What effect can we have on the place we inhabit?

Place has always been central to Lisa Sanditz’s paintings and drawings. In the winter of 2006–7, she went to China specifically to paint the rapid growth of single-industry cities, which sustained themselves by producing and exporting items such as Christmas ornaments to Western consumers. A longtime resident of the Hudson Valley, she was aware that this part of New York State, once populated by single-industry cities, such as Tannersville and Gloversville, had become post-industrial outposts for those seeking to live within hailing distance of the expensive bustle of New York City’s five boroughs. The production of inexpensive consumer goods had left America for Asia, with its cheap labor and willingness to invest in new factories.

In her current exhibition, Missing Mountain , at Alexandre Gallery — her first in New York in more than a decade — Sanditz continues to pursue her understanding of the relationship between human intervention and the landscape, paying particular attention to fitting together different pictorial languages. This postmodern approach to landscape sets her apart from her modernist forebears, from Marsden Hartley to Alex Katz , as well as implicitly acknowledges the destructive effects of climate change and greedy, unthinking human intervention. And yet, despite this awareness, Sanditz never devolves into proselytizing. Despite the gravitas of her subject matter (the degraded landscape), her pursuit is inspired by her painterly desire to celebrate beauty and what acrylic paint, and its expansive range of artificial colors, can do. Observation, memory, and imagination are inseparable components of her thinking and doing.

Marvel and Sony’s “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” involved nearly 2,000 VFX shots and just 24 weeks of post-production, with 445 shots delivered in a single week, overall VFX supervisor Jerome Chen revealed at View Conference in Turin on Wednesday.

“In one week, we did about 445 shots,” Chen said, comparing the feat with his first film as a supervisor in 1999, which contained 450 shots in total and took two years to complete.

About three-quarters of “Brand New Day’s” VFX work was delivered during the final six weeks, he added, making an already demanding schedule even more intense.

Next, Chen recalled that preparations began with a scouting trip to New York in December 2024, before he had received a finished script. Director Destin Daniel Cretton wanted a more grounded, street-level Spider-Man, with the city itself integral to the story. But most filming would take place in the U.K., where Pinewood Studios, London and Glasgow doubled for New York. Production designer Charles Wood’s concept art helped establish a relatively restrained palette, punctuated by saturated colors at key emotional moments.

The team preserved usable street-level photography and digitally replaced or extended much of what lay above it. “We just found basically a recipe of a half dozen or so things that tell you that it’s New York,” Chen said. Those included hanging traffic signals, scaffolding, water towers and the correct power lines. Even the yellow markings along British curbs had to disappear.

Small pieces of script could produce enormous technical assignments. An introduction involving Spider-Man and a tank expanded from a handful of words into 11 shots and roughly 52 seconds of footage. Physical tabletop models helped the crew determine how a vehicle should crash through a building when there was no time for elaborate previws. In another sequence, a compact camera rig mounted on a helmet captured Tom Holland’s performance from near his face, with a blurry red shape added in compositing to suggest the inside of his mask. “Sometimes the easiest tricks are the most effective,” Chen said.

The movie also gave Chen his first opportunity to work on Mark Ruffalo’s Hulk . Because the character appears in a more savage, telepathically controlled state, the team explored a different physique from earlier Marvel outings, adjusting his proportions, muscular definition, hair color and the relative size of his hands and feet. Chen consulted Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige about how Hulk’s appearance had evolved across the franchise.

“I realized that nobody had ever looked closely at Hulk’s toenails before,” Chen joked. “That was something that we had to do.” Earlier versions looked unnaturally green, while the team also considered how the character’s skin would react to different lighting. They lengthened his arms, reduced his body fat and gave him grayer hair. A subtle shift in eye color, from green to brown, signals a moment when Hulk regains his humanity. Full-scale, 10-foot Hulk standins helped actors and camera crews judge his dimensions on set, and even his pants required careful attention.

A climactic energy wave involving Jean Grey proved harder to solve creatively. Chen initially resisted the rainbow-like chromatic aberration familiar from other screen depictions of superpowers. But with five weeks remaining, he reversed course, deciding the established visual vocabulary served the film better than something overly electronic. “I thought it was the weakest part of the film,” he admitted. “I wish we had come up with something better.”

Time, he argued, often determines the quality of VFX more than the artists’ abilities. “If you go to a movie and you see that there’s a visual effects shot that doesn’t look that good, it’s not because there are bad artists on it,” he said. “You can tell they just ran out of time.” Chen advised supervisors facing decision fatigue to review shots within their sequences rather than obsess over individual frames.

Finishing so rapidly could also have consequences for the industry: “We may have done ourselves a disfavor by actually finishing this movie in 24 weeks because once again we’ve proven that it can be done on time.”

The final challenge was unexpectedly modest. With the vendors already finished, a last-minute review revealed a sweat stain under Spider-Man’s arm. “You can’t have superheroes sweating into their suit,” Chen recalled. A small team at Marvel’s Burbank offices removed it in about 47 minutes, delivered the corrected shot and sent Chen home from a nearly empty parking garage beneath the studio.
